rider.n: A rider is anyone who rides something, and the thing ridden is usually named before it: horse rider, bike rider, motorcycle rider. In American English it also means a passenger on public transport, as in bus riders or subway riders. Stress the first syllable: RI-der. Do not confuse it with writer, which sounds almost the same in fast American speech. A rider can also be an extra clause added to a contract or law, but that sense is formal and rare. For a bicycle, cyclist is the everyday alternative.
x: Every rider on the bus must hold the rail when it is crowded.
She is an experienced horse rider and has won several local prizes.
The shop gave each new rider a free helmet with the bicycle.

salespeople.n: Salespeople is the plural of salesperson and is a gender-neutral choice that has largely replaced salesman and saleswoman in business writing. It always takes a plural verb: the salespeople are meeting today. Stress the first syllable: SALES-pee-pul. Typical partners are top salespeople, retail salespeople and hire or train salespeople. Do not write salespersons unless the style guide asks for it, as it sounds stiff. In casual talk you may hear sales staff, sales reps or sales assistants, depending on the country and the type of shop.
x: The best salespeople listen carefully before they suggest a product.
Our company hires new salespeople every spring for the summer season.
Salespeople at the car dealership earn a bonus on every sale.

teller.n: Teller most often means a bank clerk who serves customers at a counter, usually written as bank teller. It comes from the verb tell in its old sense of count, which is why a teller counts money. Stress the first syllable: TEL-er. It also appears in fortune teller and storyteller, where the meaning is a person who tells. Do not confuse the bank sense with an ATM, short for automated teller machine, which is a machine rather than a person. In British English, cashier or bank clerk is a common alternative in speech.
x: Please take your check to the teller at the third window.
Her grandmother worked as a bank teller for thirty years.
The teller asked me to show my passport before opening the account.

underline.n: Underline works in two ways. Literally, you draw a line under a word on paper or screen: underline the key terms. Figuratively, it means to stress that something matters, and then the subject is usually a report, event or result: the figures underline the problem. Stress can fall on either syllable, though UN-der-line is common for the noun and un-der-LINE for the verb. The past form is underlined, regular. As an alternative, emphasize or highlight is more everyday, while underscore is a close, slightly more formal match for the figurative sense.
x: Please underline every verb in the first paragraph.
The recent accident will underline the need for better road signs.
He used a red pen to underline the mistakes in my essay.

unemployed.n: Unemployed describes a person who is able and willing to work but has no job. It is an adjective, and it can also work as a noun with the: the unemployed means unemployed people as a group, taking a plural verb. Stress the second syllable: un-em-PLOYED. Collocations include unemployed workers, the long-term unemployed and become unemployed. It is more formal and statistical than out of work or jobless, which are common in everyday talk. Avoid it for someone who has retired or chosen not to work, since the word implies a search for a job.
x: After the factory closed, hundreds of people were left unemployed.
He has been unemployed since March but is applying everywhere.
The town runs free training courses for the unemployed.

unpleasant.n: Unpleasant describes something that gives discomfort or displeasure, from a smell, taste or weather to a person or conversation. It is a mild word; with stress on the second syllable, un-PLEZ-ent, it can sound polite where nasty or disgusting would sound rude. People say an unpleasant surprise, an unpleasant task or unpleasant weather. About a person, it means unfriendly or rude, so he was very unpleasant to the waiter is a clear complaint. Its opposite is pleasant. Do not shorten it to unpleased, which is not a normal word for this idea.
x: There was an unpleasant smell coming from the kitchen.
Telling him the bad news was an unpleasant job for the manager.
The weather turned unpleasant, so we went back inside.

unused.n: Unused is an adjective for something that has not been used, such as unused tickets, unused land or unused vacation days. Stress the second syllable and say un-YOOZD. Watch out for a second word, spelled the same but said un-YOOST, which means not accustomed to: she is unused to the cold. Context usually shows which one is meant. The past participle is the same form, as in the tickets went unused. Alternatives include spare or new, depending on the object, and idle for machines and land.
x: Return any unused medicine to the pharmacy for safe disposal.
The old factory stood unused for ten years before it was sold.
I am unused to getting up this early, so I feel tired.

walkway.n: A walkway is a path or passage made for people on foot, often raised, covered or running beside something else, such as a bridge, a building or a garden. The stress is on the first syllable: WALK-way. Common partners are pedestrian walkway, covered walkway and clear the walkway. It is a countable noun, so you can say two walkways. It is more specific than path, which can be a natural track, and less general than sidewalk or pavement, which run beside a road. Safety signs often use it in the phrase keep walkways clear.
x: A glass walkway links the two towers on the fifth floor.
Please do not park bikes on the walkway outside the school.
The garden has a gravel walkway lined with small lamps.

yearly.n: Yearly can be an adjective or an adverb, and the form does not change. As an adjective it sits before a noun: a yearly fee, a yearly checkup. As an adverb it follows the verb: the festival is held yearly. It means once every year, so it is nearly the same as annual, which sounds a little more formal and official, as in an annual report. Stress the first syllable: YEER-lee. It can also mean per year, as in a yearly income of fifty thousand dollars. In speech, every year is the most natural choice.
x: The gym charges a yearly fee that is cheaper than paying monthly.
Our family visits the lake yearly in the last week of July.
Her yearly income rose after she changed jobs.

donor.n: A donor is a person who gives something, most often blood, an organ or money to a charity. The stress is on the first syllable: DOH-ner. Typical collocations are blood donor, organ donor, kidney donor and a generous donor. The matching word for the person who receives is recipient. Notice the spelling, because donor ends in -or, not -er. The verb is donate, and the noun for the act is donation. In fundraising talk, a donor is also a supporter who gives regularly, so charities often write about thanking their donors.
x: The clinic is looking for a donor with a rare blood type.
An anonymous donor paid for the new playground.
He signed up as an organ donor when he renewed his license.

hydraulic.n: Hydraulic is a technical adjective for machines or systems that use pressure in a liquid, usually oil, to move or lift things. Stress the second syllable: hy-DRAW-lik. It nearly always comes before a noun: hydraulic brakes, hydraulic press, hydraulic fluid, hydraulic lift. Do not mix it up with pneumatic, which uses air or gas instead of liquid. In engineering it can also describe water flow, as in hydraulic engineering for dams and pipes. There is no everyday substitute; in simple speech you might say run by oil pressure or fluid power.
x: The truck uses a hydraulic arm to lift heavy loads onto the shelf.
A leak in the hydraulic line made the brakes feel soft.
Mechanics check the hydraulic fluid level during every service.

integer.n: An integer is a whole number that has no fraction or decimal part, and it can be positive, negative or zero. Examples are minus three, zero and forty-two. Say IN-ti-jer, with the stress on the first syllable and a soft j. It is a standard term in maths and programming, where an integer variable stores whole numbers only and integer overflow happens when a value gets too big. Do not use it for a decimal such as 2.5. Everyday alternatives are whole number or just number, and the adjective is integral only in a different, general sense.
x: Enter an integer between one and ten to continue.
Dividing seven by two does not give an integer result.
The program stores each score as an integer to save memory.

lubrication.n: Lubrication is the process of putting oil, grease or another slippery substance between moving parts so they rub less and wear out more slowly. It is an uncountable noun, so we say regular lubrication, not a lubrication. Stress the third syllable: loo-bri-KAY-shun. Related words are the verb lubricate and the noun lubricant, which is the substance itself. Typical phrases include lubrication system, poor lubrication and lubrication schedule. It is technical, mostly used in engineering and maintenance. In plain speech, people say oiling or greasing a machine, a chain or a hinge.
x: Poor lubrication caused the bearings to overheat and fail.
The manual gives a lubrication schedule for every moving part.
Check the lubrication of the chain before each long ride.

pharmacology.n: Pharmacology is the scientific study of how drugs work in the body and how the body responds to them. It is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb: pharmacology is a difficult subject. Stress the fourth syllable: far-muh-KOL-uh-jee. You will meet it in phrases such as clinical pharmacology, a pharmacology course and pharmacology research. Do not mix it up with pharmacy, which is a shop or the work of preparing and giving out medicines. A person who studies it is a pharmacologist. In simple terms, you can say the science of medicines.
x: She is studying pharmacology because she wants to design new drugs.
The pharmacology of this painkiller is well understood.
A pharmacology textbook explains how doses are calculated.

physiology.n: Physiology is the branch of biology that studies how living bodies and their parts work, such as the heart, lungs and muscles. It is uncountable and takes a singular verb. Stress the third syllable: fiz-ee-OL-uh-jee. Common phrases are human physiology, exercise physiology and plant physiology. The person who studies it is a physiologist, and the adjective is physiological. Do not confuse it with physics or with psychology, which sound similar. Physiology can also mean the way a particular body works, as in the physiology of a snake. Anatomy deals with structure, while physiology deals with function.
x: Students of physiology learn how muscles use energy during exercise.
The physiology of birds allows them to fly at high altitude.
He took a physiology exam before starting his sports degree.

physiotherapy.n: Physiotherapy is treatment for injury or illness that uses exercise, massage and movement rather than drugs or surgery. It is a British term, and in the United States physical therapy is the usual name, so both are worth knowing. The noun is uncountable: she needs physiotherapy, not a physiotherapy. Stress the third syllable: fiz-ee-oh-THER-uh-pee. Informally, people shorten it to physio, and the professional is a physiotherapist. Typical phrases are have physiotherapy, a physiotherapy clinic and physiotherapy after surgery. It aims to restore movement and reduce pain.
x: After her knee operation she went to physiotherapy twice a week.
The hospital has a physiotherapy room with special equipment.
Regular physiotherapy can prevent back pain from returning.

pneumatic.n: Pneumatic describes tools and machines driven by compressed air or gas, such as a pneumatic drill or a pneumatic hammer. The first letter p is silent, so say noo-MAT-ik, with the stress on the second syllable. It comes before a noun in nearly every case: pneumatic tyre, pneumatic cylinder, pneumatic system. Do not confuse it with hydraulic, which relies on liquid under pressure. It can also mean filled with air, as in pneumatic tyres on a bicycle. In simple speech you might say air-powered, and the noun pneumatics names the field of study.
x: Workers used a pneumatic drill to break up the old concrete.
The doors open and close with a small pneumatic cylinder.
Pneumatic brakes are common on large trains and heavy trucks.

radiotherapy.n: Radiotherapy is the treatment of disease, above all cancer, using controlled beams of radiation to damage and kill harmful cells. It is uncountable: she is having radiotherapy. Stress the third syllable: ray-dee-oh-THER-uh-pee. Typical combinations are receive radiotherapy, a course of radiotherapy and radiotherapy and chemotherapy. In the United States people may say radiation therapy, and doctors also use the short form radiation. Do not confuse it with chemotherapy, which uses drugs rather than radiation. The specialist is a radiotherapist or a radiation oncologist, and the treatment is given in short daily sessions.
x: After the operation he began a course of radiotherapy at the cancer center.
Radiotherapy can make patients feel very tired for several weeks.
The doctor explained how radiotherapy targets only the tumor.

troubleshooting.n: Troubleshooting is the step by step search for the cause of a fault, so that it can be fixed. It is an uncountable noun and often appears before another noun: a troubleshooting guide, troubleshooting steps, network troubleshooting. Stress the first syllable: TRUB-ul-shoot-ing. The verb is troubleshoot, and the person is a troubleshooter. It is used in IT, engineering and customer support. Do not confuse it with simply repairing; it focuses on diagnosis, finding out what is wrong. In casual talk, working out what is wrong or figuring out the problem are everyday alternatives.
x: The help page includes a troubleshooting guide for common Wi-Fi problems.
Troubleshooting the printer took longer than replacing it would have.
Good troubleshooting starts by checking the simplest cause first.

virtualization.n: Virtualization means creating a software version of something physical, such as a server, a storage device or a network, so that one machine can act as many. It is uncountable and mainly used in computing. Stress the second syllable: vur-chuh-wuh-ly-ZAY-shun. British spelling is virtualisation. Typical phrases are server virtualization, virtualization software and cloud virtualization. The verb is virtualize, and the product is a virtual machine. Do not confuse it with virtual reality, which is a simulated world for users. For people outside IT, you could say running several computers inside one.
x: Virtualization lets small firms avoid buying a separate server for every task.
The IT team moved the old systems to virtualization last year.
Our course covers virtualization, networks and basic security.

inexpensive.n: Inexpensive means low in price, and it carries a positive feeling: good value without being poor quality. It is different from cheap, which can suggest low quality. So the writer of a travel site will say inexpensive hotels, but a shabby jacket may be called cheap. Stress the second syllable: in-ik-SPEN-siv. Typical partners are inexpensive option, relatively inexpensive and fairly inexpensive. Notice the spelling, which is in- plus expensive. Alternatives are affordable, reasonable and budget. The opposite is expensive or costly.
x: We found an inexpensive restaurant near the station.
Cotton is an inexpensive material, so the shirts sell for very little.
Solar lamps are now inexpensive enough for most villages to buy.

lightweight.n: Lightweight describes things that weigh little for their size or kind, as in a lightweight jacket, a lightweight laptop or a lightweight frame. It can be one word or, in some styles, light-weight, but one word is standard now. Stress usually falls on the first syllable: LITE-wayt. It is generally a positive word for goods. Used about a person or an idea, it is critical: a lightweight argument means it lacks depth. As a noun it also names a boxing class. A plainer alternative for objects is light, and the opposite is heavy.
x: Pack a lightweight raincoat because it may shower in the afternoon.
The tent is lightweight, so one person can carry it easily.
Critics called the film a lightweight story with a weak ending.

nap.n: A nap is a short sleep, usually in the daytime, and it is lighter and shorter than a full night of sleep. The common verb phrase is take a nap, and Americans also say catch a nap. You can have a quick nap, an afternoon nap or a power nap. It can also be a verb: the baby naps after lunch. The spelling doubles the p before endings: napping, napped. In the phrase caught napping it means caught unprepared. Informal alternatives include snooze and forty winks, and doze means to sleep lightly.
x: The baby usually takes a nap after lunch.
A twenty-minute nap helps me concentrate during the afternoon.
Grandpa fell asleep on the sofa during his Sunday nap.

pastry.n: Pastry has two uses. As an uncountable noun it means the dough of flour, fat and water used for pies and tarts: shortcrust pastry, puff pastry. As a countable noun it means a small sweet baked item, such as a croissant or a Danish; here you say a pastry, two pastries. The plural changes y to ies. Stress the first syllable: PAY-stree. A person who makes them is a pastry chef. Do not confuse it with paste. In everyday talk, many people say cake or baked treat for the sweet items.
x: The bakery sells fresh pastry every morning before eight.
She chose a cream-filled pastry from the glass counter.
Roll the pastry thinly before you put it in the dish.

rewrite.n: Rewrite means to write something again, usually to improve or correct it, as in rewrite an essay or rewrite a contract. It is irregular: rewrite, rewrote, rewritten. Stress the second syllable as a verb, ree-RITE, but the noun, a rewrite, is stressed on the first: REE-rite, as in the editor wanted a rewrite. It takes a direct object and often comes with from scratch or completely. It is more thorough than edit, which means to change a little, and close to revise. Everyday alternative: write it again.
x: The teacher asked us to rewrite the conclusion in simpler words.
He had to rewrite the whole report after the data changed.
The author will rewrite the final chapter before publication.

rug.n: A rug is a piece of thick material, often woven, that covers part of a floor, usually smaller than a carpet, which covers a whole room. You can say a wool rug, an area rug or a Persian rug. Stress is simple, since it is one syllable: rhymes with bug. The phrase pull the rug out from under someone means to take away their support suddenly. In British English, a rug can also be a blanket for the knees or for picnics. It also has an informal use meaning a wig, but that is dated and jokey.
x: We put a soft rug beside the bed to keep our feet warm.
The cat sleeps on the rug in front of the fireplace.
She bought a handmade rug at the market in Istanbul.

scenery.n: Scenery is an uncountable noun for the natural views of a place, such as hills, forests, coast and sky, especially when they look attractive. Because it is uncountable, you cannot say sceneries; use scenery, or a piece of scenery. Stress the first syllable: SEE-nuh-ree. Typical phrases are beautiful scenery, mountain scenery, stunning scenery and enjoy the scenery. In theater it also means the painted backgrounds on a stage. Do not mix it up with scene, which is a single event or view. In casual talk, view or views is a common alternative for what you see from a window.
x: The scenery along the coast road is simply stunning.
We stopped twice to enjoy the scenery and take photos.
The play had cheap scenery, but the acting was excellent.

silently.n: Silently is an adverb meaning without any sound or without speaking: she waited silently, they worked silently. It comes from silent, and the stress is on the first syllable: SY-lent-lee. It often follows a verb or sits before it for effect, as in silently he left the room. A phone on silent can be said to be set to vibrate silently, but silent as an adjective is better for settings: silent mode. It is close to quietly, though quietly means with little noise, while silently means none at all. Another alternative is in silence.
x: The students sat silently while the teacher read the results.
He silently closed the door so the baby would not wake.
The cat moved silently across the dark kitchen floor.

smoothly.n: Smoothly is an adverb that means without problems or sudden stops, and it is used for processes as well as movement. Say run smoothly, go smoothly or work smoothly, especially about plans, engines, systems and events. Stress the first syllable: SMOOTH-lee, with the th sound voiced as in this. It can also describe a surface or a manner: she spoke smoothly. Do not use it as an adjective; the adjective is smooth. Everyday alternatives include without a hitch and easily. The negative would be badly or with difficulty.
x: The new software runs smoothly even on an old computer.
Everything went smoothly at the airport, and we boarded on time.
The driver brought the bus to a stop very smoothly.

tile.n: A tile is a thin, flat piece of baked clay, stone, plastic or similar material used to cover floors, walls and roofs. It is countable, so you say a tile, many tiles, and we also use it as a verb: tile the kitchen floor. Common phrases are floor tile, roof tile, ceramic tile and a tile floor. The word appears in games too, such as the tiles in Scrabble or mahjong. In British English, a tiled roof is common. The plain alternative for the verb is to cover with tiles, and for the noun there is no simpler everyday word.
x: One tile cracked when the heavy box fell on the floor.
They will tile the bathroom walls with white ceramic squares.
The old house has a red tile roof that is almost a century old.

vacuum.n: As a verb, vacuum means to clean a floor, carpet or sofa using a machine that sucks up dust: vacuum the stairs. It is regular, vacuumed and vacuuming, and note the double u in the spelling. Stress the first syllable: VAK-yoom. In everyday American English, the machine is a vacuum, while British people say hoover, from a brand, or vacuum cleaner. As a noun it also means a space with no air, and a vacuum can mean an empty gap, as in a power vacuum. The common alternative in Britain is hoover or clean the carpet.
x: Please vacuum the living room before the guests arrive.
I need to vacuum under the sofa, because there is dust everywhere.
He vacuumed the car seats after the family trip.

wool.n: Wool is the soft, thick hair of sheep and some other animals, and also the thread or cloth made from it. It is uncountable, so we say some wool, not a wool, unless a type is meant. It is said with a short oo like in book: wul. Typical partners are pure wool, merino wool, wool sweater and wool coat. Be careful with the spelling, as double o and not double l at the start. The adjective is woolen, or woollen in British English. The phrase pull the wool over someone's eyes means to deceive them. Cotton and fleece are other fabrics.
x: This scarf is soft because it is made of fine merino wool.
The farmer sells wool from his sheep to a factory in town.
A thick wool blanket kept us warm in the cold cabin.

decree.n: A decree is an official order from a ruler or government that has the force of law, often without a vote in parliament. You issue, sign or pass a decree, and the phrase by decree means by official order. Stress the second syllable: di-KREE. It is also a verb: the king decreed a holiday. A court decree is a judge's decision, for example a divorce decree. It is formal and used in news and law, while order, ruling or regulation are plainer. Do not confuse it with degree, which has a different meaning and spelling.
x: The president signed a decree that closed the border for a week.
Under the new decree, all shops must close by midnight.
The judge issued a decree ending the long dispute over the land.

disinfect.n: Disinfect means to clean something with a chemical so that germs are destroyed, for example a wound, a kitchen counter or a toilet. It takes an object: disinfect the surface. Stress the third syllable: dis-in-FEKT. The noun is disinfectant, the substance used, and disinfection is the process. It is stronger than clean, which only removes dirt, and close to sanitize, which lowers germs to a safe level. Typical phrases include disinfect hands, disinfect equipment and disinfect a cut. Everyday alternative: clean with bleach or antiseptic.
x: Always disinfect the cutting board after you prepare raw chicken.
The nurse used a cloth to disinfect the cut on my knee.
Teachers disinfect the desks every evening during flu season.

grinding.n: Grinding is the process of shaping, smoothing or sharpening a material using a hard rotating wheel or by crushing it into powder. In engineering it is uncountable: surface grinding, precision grinding, a grinding wheel. Stress the first syllable: GRYN-ding. As an adjective it also describes harsh scraping sounds or exhausting effort, as in a grinding noise or grinding poverty. It comes from the verb grind, ground, ground, which is irregular. Do not confuse the two meanings; in a coffee shop, grinding refers to making the beans into powder. Casual alternatives: sharpening or polishing.
x: Grinding removes a very thin layer of metal from the part.
A grinding noise from the engine told him something was wrong.
Fine grinding of the beans makes the coffee taste stronger.
